final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Starting. Scoping to exactly the three things you asked for: (1) DIY vs. hire recommendation, (2) 2–3 South Bay trainers with real prices, (3) a week-by-week 4-week plan. Breaking it into subtasks now, then researching.

Note on the behavior: 14-month-old rescue BC mix + pulling + barking at every dog is a very common combination — the barking is almost certainly leash reactivity (frustration or fear), not aggression, and the pulling makes it worse. That framing will drive the recommendation.

comments.body:
Done — report attached. All three questions answered, nothing researched beyond them.

**1. Hire or DIY?** Both, but weighted to DIY. This is leash reactivity (frustration/over-arousal), not aggression — the trainable version. Do the daily work yourself; buy exactly one thing you can't manufacture on a sidewalk: a class with staged dogs behind barriers at a controlled distance. Skip the $2,400–$6,600 private and day-training tiers for now.

**2. Trainers.** Three force-free options with real prices:
- **South Bay Dog Training, Campbell — $360**, 5 weeks, Sunday mornings. Best value, and the class is scoped exactly to dogs who are fine off-leash but struggle on-leash. (408) 429-8132.
- **D For Dogz — $510**, nine sessions over 5 weeks, Mountain View Saturdays. First two sessions are people-only, which is the right way round. 650-538-3011.
- **In Tune Dog Training** — strongest credentials, sliding scale under $115K/yr, pricing unpublished. Hold in reserve.

Screened out Off Leash K9 (e-collar based) and, reluctantly, HSSV — they state on their own site that a dog who lunges on leash and can't be refocused isn't right for their group classes.

**3. Four-week plan.** Five subtasks: Week 0 (gear + stop rehearsing the barking), then Weeks 1–4. The spine is: measure his threshold distance in week 1 and write the number down, run engage-disengage below that distance in short 1–5 minute sessions, then compare week 4 against week 1 on distance, outbursts per walk, and recovery time.

**One thing is time-sensitive.** South Bay Dog Training's Sunday 11 AM reactive class is full, but they'll open a 12 PM section if two people ask. Email southbaydogtrainers@gmail.com this week — that's the whole ask. Everything else can wait.

Parent set to needs_review. All five week-subtasks are assigned to you and sit not_started; the trainer research is done and its remaining child is the phone/email step.

One judgement call I made without you: I assumed he's OK with other dogs *off* leash, since both candidate classes require that. Verify before you book — if he's reactive off-leash too, go straight to In Tune for a 1:1 instead.

report.markdown:
# Training plan: 14-month rescue border collie mix, South Bay CA

**Short version:** don't buy a $2,400 private package. Start training yourself this weekend, spend $360 on one reactive-dog group class in Campbell, and re-assess in four weeks against a number you write down in week one.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or do it yourself?

**Both — DIY as the daily work, one group class as the paid component.**

Your dog is showing textbook **leash reactivity**, not aggression. <cite index="53-1">Reactivity shows up as intense barking, lunging, or pulling in response to everyday things like other dogs, driven by fear, frustration, or lack of self-control rather than intent to harm — and distinguishing it from true aggression is key when deciding what professional help you need.</cite> A 14-month herding-breed adolescent barking at *every* dog, not selectively, is the classic frustrated/over-aroused profile: peak adolescent arousal plus a leash that stops him resolving the situation himself.

That matters, because it's the version of the problem an owner can actually train.

### Why DIY is the right base layer

1. **The pulling and the barking are one problem.** A dog at the end of a taut leash cannot be turned away from an oncoming dog. Loose-leash walking is the mechanism that makes everything else possible — and it's ordinary training you don't need to pay $250/hour for.
2. **The protocol is public and well-documented.** <cite index="59-2,59-3">The engage-disengage game has two levels: the first rewards the dog for engaging with the trigger while not showing a stress response, building positive feelings toward it; the second rewards the dog for turning away — a behaviour physically incompatible with barking and lunging at it.</cite>
3. **Cost.** Group class $360–$510. Private coaching $2,400. Day training $4,200–$6,600. Nothing here suggests you need the expensive tier yet.
4. **Frequency beats intensity.** This is short daily reps below threshold. A trainer you see weekly can't do that for you — you're doing the work either way.

### The one thing you genuinely can't DIY

Safe, controlled exposure to another dog at a distance *you* choose. On a public sidewalk, dogs appear too close, too fast. A reactive class stages dogs behind visual barriers at a set distance. That's what the $360 buys, and it's worth it.

### The decision point — run this in week 1

<cite index="41-3,41-4,41-5">Walk him carrying high-value treats (chicken, hot dog, cheese) and see whether you can get his attention when you pass another dog. If you can easily redirect him with treats in hand, you can go straight into ordinary training. If it's difficult to get his focus back even with high-value food, the dedicated reactive-dog class is the right level.</cite>

<cite index="42-4">Escalate to a professional if you cannot find any distance at which he stays under threshold, if the behaviour is clearly fear-based and intense rather than excited frustration, if it's escalating despite your efforts, or if you suspect it's tipping from reactivity into aggression.</cite>

### Non-negotiable

No prong collar, no choke chain, no e-collar, no leash corrections. <cite index="42-4">For reactivity specifically, look for reward-based methods and a trainer who understands thresholds and counterconditioning, and avoid the punishment and correction tools that make reactivity worse.</cite> This rules out one local operator (below).

---

## 2. Local options, with real prices

| | South Bay Dog Training | D For Dogz | In Tune Dog Training |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Where** | 186 E Sunnyoaks Ave, Ste C, Campbell | Mountain View venue; serves whole South Bay | In-home, ~15 mi of Cambrian, San Jose |
| **Group reactive class** | **$360** | **$510** | none |
| **What that includes** | <cite index="63-1">5 weeks: 4× 45-min in-person + 5× 45-min weekly Zoom Q&A + daily support group</cite> | <cite index="66-1">Nine 60-min sessions over 5 weeks — five in-person, four Zoom</cite> | — |
| **When** | Sunday mornings; <cite index="66-2">Zoom Q&A Tuesdays 7 PM</cite> | <cite index="66-2">Sat 2–3 PM class, Thu 6:30 PM Zoom</cite> | Weekends on request |
| **Private** | Drop-in $75 | <cite index="66-2">$420 consult + $250/session; 5 for $1,250, 10 for $2,400</cite> | Not published (~$150 consult, unconfirmed) |
| **Contact** | (408) 429-8132 · southbaydogtrainers@gmail.com | 650-538-3011 | nancy@intunedogtraining.com |

### ⭐ Pick: South Bay Dog Training — Reactive Dog Level 1, $360

Best price, right format, and the class scope matches your dog precisely. <cite index="63-2">Their group class is designed for dogs that do well with other dogs off-leash but struggle with dogs on-leash — not for dogs aggressive both on and off leash.</cite> They also frame the problem correctly: <cite index="63-3">growling, jumping and lunging at the sight of another dog is not uncommon and is often caused by the restriction of the leash.</cite>

- <cite index="63-2">Training happens in their Campbell centre with barriers that help with the visual trigger.</cite>
- <cite index="63-2">Flat collar, martingale or harness only — no prong, choke or e-collars; 6 ft non-retractable leash.</cite> Exactly the standard you want.
- <cite index="63-2">Requires proof of one DHPP vaccine; dogs 16 weeks or older; no make-up classes.</cite>
- **Time-sensitive:** <cite index="63-2">the Sunday 11:00 AM section is full, but they've said they'll add a 12:00 PM class if two people ask — they need two participants to start.</cite> Email them this week.
- Level 2 ($360) takes it outdoors afterwards — that's your month 2–3.

### Runner-up: D For Dogz — $510

More expensive, but structurally excellent. <cite index="66-2">The first two in-person classes are people-only</cite> — they teach the handler before involving the dog, which is the right order. They also run a **free** reactive-dog owner support group open to non-clients. One catch: the cohort date posted on their site is stale, so call for the current start date. Skip the $4,200 day-training and $6,600 intensive tiers — nothing about your dog justifies them yet.

### Escalation option: In Tune Dog Training

<cite index="46-1">Nancy Le is an Academy for Dog Trainers graduate specialising in fear and aggression</cite>, using <cite index="46-2">reward-based methods with no corrections, shock, choke, or prongs</cite> — the strongest credentials of the three. <cite index="49-1">Tiered pricing is available for households earning under $115K/year, and weekend appointments may be available on request.</cite> Pricing isn't published; ask. Call her if the week-1 threshold test fails.

### Ruled out

- **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** — <cite index="52-1">$500 for the first lesson including an e-collar, then $100/session.</cite> Aversive tools on a fear/frustration-driven dog. Don't.
- **Zoom Room Santa Clara** — genuinely force-free, ~$199/mo, but it's a group obedience gym with dogs sharing a room. Wrong environment for a dog currently over threshold at the sight of any dog. Revisit later.
- **Humane Society Silicon Valley** — cheapest at $200/6 weeks, but they say it themselves: <cite index="55-2">if your dog barks, growls and lunges on leash at another dog and can't be refocused, he may not be appropriate for their group classes</cite>, and that behaviour <cite index="55-2">both stops your dog learning and unsettles the other dogs.</cite>

---

## 3. The four-week plan

Each week is its own subtask in the tree with full drill-by-drill detail. Summary:

### Week 0 — this weekend
Buy: front-clip harness, 6 ft non-retractable leash, clicker, high-value treats, belt treat pouch.

Then **stop the rehearsal**. Every barking episode strengthens the behaviour and floods him with stress hormones that take days to clear. For two weeks, walk at dawn/after dark, or drive to an empty field. If a dog appears, U-turn and leave *before* the outburst. Replace walks with sniffing and chewing work — scatter-feeding, snuffle mat, food puzzles, 15 min/day.

### Week 1 — measure, don't train triggers
Run the threshold test and **write the number down in feet**. <cite index="60-1">For most leash-reactive dogs the starting threshold is 50–100 feet from another dog.</cite> That number is your baseline and your proof of progress.

Daily 5–10 min, no dogs present: name game, "find it", fast U-turn, loose-leash in the driveway. <cite index="59-1">Practise fast U-turns by luring with a treat at his nose or tossing "find it" treats on the ground as you change direction.</cite>

*Success:* you know your distance; head snaps round on his name 9/10 indoors; 10 slack-leash steps down the driveway.

### Week 2 — engage-disengage begins
<cite index="59-1">Level 1: stand at your working distance, be quiet and still so he notices the trigger himself. The moment he looks at it, click; when he turns back to you, treat. If he reacts or doesn't turn back, move further away and reset. Aim for 3–5 successful reps in a row before moving on.</cite>

<cite index="59-1">Level 2: let him notice, then wait 1–5 seconds to see if he looks away on his own. Click the instant he disengages, then treat. If he fixates longer than 5 seconds, drop back to Level 1. After 3–5 clean reps, move 1–5 steps closer.</cite>

**Dosage matters more than people expect.** <cite index="59-1">Play for 1–5 minutes, then take a break.</cite> Two or three sessions a week. <cite index="61-1">Prolonged exposure — even at sub-threshold distances — accumulates stress, so keep sessions brief and positive.</cite>

Back off at the *early* signals, not the bark: <cite index="59-1">lip-licking, yawning, or scratching out of context.</cite>

*Success:* he looks at a distant dog and back at you for a treat; you've shaved 10–20 ft off week 1.

### Week 3 — class starts
Bring your week-1 number to the first session. Continue engage-disengage 2–3×/week. Add: the emergency U-turn rehearsed cold with no dog present (5× per walk until *your* hands know it), the 1-2-3 pattern game, and parallel walking with a friend's calm dog — same direction, 50+ ft apart, gradually converging, never head-on.

*Success:* you can pass a stationary dog at roughly half the week-1 distance with him eating and checking in; the U-turn is automatic.

### Week 4 — real walks, then decide
Two or three normal-time neighbourhood walks using management: cross early, put parked cars between you, duck into driveways. Compare against week 1 on three numbers:

| Metric | Week 1 | Week 4 |
|---|---|---|
| Working distance (ft) | | |
| Outbursts per walk | | |
| Recovery time after an outburst | | |

Recovery time usually improves *before* the barking does — watch it closely.

- **Improving →** book Level 2 ($360) and keep going.
- **Flat or worse →** book private 1:1, and see a vet. Pain, thyroid issues and chronic under-sleep all lower the reactivity threshold, and adolescent dogs are frequently under-slept.

---

## Expectations

Four weeks buys you a measurable drop in working distance and a handler who knows what to do. It does not buy a fixed dog — realistically that's 3–6 months.

And set the target honestly. <cite index="59-4">If he's triggered by other dogs, it's worth acknowledging he may not be destined to be a dog-park dog — some dogs simply prefer human company or have more introverted social personalities.</cite> <cite index="59-4">In many cases, working up to walking past another dog calmly on-leash is a perfectly acceptable goal for both of you.</cite> That is the win. Aim at it.

---

## Do this first

Email **southbaydogtrainers@gmail.com** to get on the waitlist for the 12:00 PM Reactive Dog 1 section. They need two people to open it, so you're competing with a clock. Everything else can wait a week.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Do a hybrid — start DIY this weekend, and book ONE group reactive-dog class as the paid component. Do not buy a $2,400–$6,600 private/day-training package at this stage.

Reasoning:

1. This is almost certainly leash reactivity, not aggression. Barking and lunging at every dog is driven by frustration, fear, or over-arousal rather than intent to harm, and it is a different problem from true aggression. A 14-month adolescent border collie mix that barks at EVERY dog (not selectively) and pulls hard is the classic frustrated-greeter / over-aroused profile — a herding breed at peak adolescent arousal with a leash preventing it from resolving the situation.

2. It is a DIY-tractable case IF you can find a working distance. The standard test: walk with high-value treats and see whether you can get the dog's attention when another dog is visible. If you can redirect at some distance, the dog is trainable at threshold and the protocols (engage-disengage / counterconditioning) work in an owner's hands. Professional help becomes necessary if you cannot find ANY distance where the dog stays under threshold, if it's clearly fear-based and intense rather than excited frustration, if it's escalating despite effort, or if it is tipping into real aggression. Do the distance test in week 1 — it is the single decision point.

3. The pulling and the barking are the same problem and DIY fixes them together. A dog that pulls has no loose-leash default to fall back on when a trigger appears; you cannot execute a U-turn away from another dog when the dog is at the end of a taut leash. Loose-leash walking is very ordinary training you do not need to pay $250/hour for.

4. Where a pro genuinely adds value, and why the class format: the hard part of reactivity work is (a) reading the dog's early stress signals before the explosion and (b) getting safe, controlled exposure to another dog at a distance you control. You cannot manufacture (b) on a public sidewalk — real dogs appear too close, too fast. A structured reactive class provides staged dogs behind barriers at a chosen distance. That is the one thing you cannot DIY.

5. Cost logic. A reactive-dog group class in the South Bay is $360–$510. Private coaching is $2,400+ and day training is $4,200–$6,600. There is no evidence this dog needs the expensive tier; buy the cheap tier first and escalate only if week 1's distance test fails.

ESCALATE TO PRIVATE 1:1 IF, within the first 4 weeks, any of these are true:
- There is no distance, even across a wide street or park, at which the dog can notice another dog and take a treat.
- The dog redirects onto you — grabs the leash, mouths your arms, spins and bites at clothing during an outburst.
- The dog cannot recover within a minute or two after an outburst, or is visibly wound up for the rest of the walk.
- Any snap or bite toward a dog or person.
In those cases go to In Tune Dog Training (Academy for Dog Trainers credential, sliding scale available) rather than to a board-and-train.

WHAT NOT TO DO: no prong collar, no choke chain, no e-collar, no leash-popping, no "correcting" the bark. Punishing the bark suppresses the warning without changing the underlying fear or frustration, and reactivity commonly worsens. This rules out Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose and any "balanced" trainer.

subtasks.title: Write the week-by-week plan for weeks 1–4
subtasks.description:
Plan written. Broken into five child subtasks: Week 0 (kit + stop the rehearsal), then Weeks 1–4, each with daily drills, dosage, and a written "success looks like" checkpoint. Full detail lives in those children and in the report on the parent task.

Structure of the plan:
- Wk 0: gear (front-clip harness, 6ft non-retractable leash, clicker, high-value treats, treat pouch) + trigger avoidance so the barking stops being rehearsed. Enrichment substitutes for walks.
- Wk 1: measure the working distance (the key number), name game, "find it", U-turn, loose leash indoors/driveway.
- Wk 2: engage-disengage protocol (Karen Pryor levels 1 and 2) at the working distance, 1–5 min per session, 2–3x/week.
- Wk 3: reactive class starts; emergency U-turn rehearsed cold; 1-2-3 pattern game; parallel walking with a neutral dog.
- Wk 4: real-world walks with management; review distance/outbursts/recovery time vs week 1; decide whether to continue DIY+class or escalate to 1:1.

Two design decisions worth flagging:
1. Pulling and barking are trained together, not sequentially — the loose-leash work exists so the U-turn is physically possible when a dog appears.
2. The plan is deliberately low-volume. Short, frequent, sub-threshold sessions beat long ones; stress accumulates even below threshold and an over-worked reactive dog regresses.

Realistic horizon: meaningful change in 3–6 months. Four weeks buys a measurable drop in working distance and a handler who knows what to do, not a fixed dog.

subtasks.title: Week 0 (this weekend): buy the kit and stop the rehearsal
subtasks.description:
Before any training. Two jobs.

BUY:
- Front-clip / Y-front harness (Balance, Freedom, or Perfect Fit). Clips at the chest so pulling turns the dog rather than letting them lean into it. NO prong, choke, or e-collar — the class you'll enrol in bans them at the door anyway.
- 6 ft flat leash. NOT retractable — retractables make it impossible to control distance, which is the whole game here.
- A clicker, or pick a marker word ('yes') and use it consistently.
- High-value treats: real chicken, cheese, hot dog, freeze-dried liver. Kibble will not compete with another dog at 40 feet.
- A treat pouch that clips to your belt. Fumbling in a pocket costs you the timing.

STOP THE REHEARSAL (this is half the battle):
Every walk where the dog barks and lunges makes the behaviour stronger and floods them with stress hormones that take days to clear. For the next 2 weeks, do not walk anywhere you'll meet dogs at close range. Walk at 6am or after dark, drive to an empty school field or industrial park, use a quiet cul-de-sac. If a dog appears, U-turn and leave before the outburst — do not push through it.

A border collie mix that isn't getting walked needs an outlet: 15 min/day of scatter-feeding in grass, a snuffle mat, food puzzles, and short trick sessions. Sniffing and chewing genuinely lower arousal; a tired-but-frantic dog is worse than a rested one.

subtasks.title: Week 1: threshold test + name game + loose leash indoors
subtasks.description:
Goal for the week: find out how far away another dog has to be before your dog can still think, and build the two mechanical skills you'll need later. No trigger work at close range at all this week.

THE THRESHOLD TEST (do this once, day 1 or 2, and write the number down):
Go somewhere you can see dogs from far away — edge of a park, across a wide street, a parking lot overlooking a trail. Stand still with high-value treats. When a dog comes into view, note whether yours can (a) look at it and (b) take a treat from your hand. If yes, step 10 ft closer next time. If no, back up until yes. The distance where the answer is still 'yes' is your working distance. It is commonly 50–100 ft for a leash-reactive dog. WRITE IT DOWN — it is your baseline and the number that proves progress.
If there is NO distance at which the dog will take food, stop and escalate to a private trainer (see the escalation criteria in the 'hire vs DIY' subtask).

DAILY, 5–10 MIN, indoors/backyard, no dogs present:
1. Name game / check-in: say the dog's name once, mark the instant they look at you, treat. 20 reps. This is the emergency handbrake you'll use later.
2. 'Find it': toss a treat on the ground and say 'find it'. Repeat until the phrase alone makes the dog drop their nose. This is how you get their head down and away from a dog that appeared too close.
3. Fast U-turn: with the dog on leash, say 'this way', lure with a treat at their nose, pivot 180 degrees, treat as they follow. 10 reps. Make it a cheerful game so it isn't scary later.
4. Loose leash, indoors then driveway: take one step; if the leash is slack, mark and treat at your trouser seam. If it tightens, stop dead — do not pull back — wait for slack, then move again. Two minutes at a time.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: you know your working distance in feet; dog whips their head round on their name 9 times out of 10 indoors; dog does 10 steps down the driveway on a slack leash.

subtasks.title: Week 2: start engage-disengage at your working distance
subtasks.description:
Goal: change how the dog FEELS about seeing another dog, at a distance where they can still think. This is the core protocol and it is exactly what a reactive class charges you for.

ENGAGE–DISENGAGE (Karen Pryor / clickertraining.com). Two levels:
LEVEL 1 – ENGAGE: Stand at your working distance. Be quiet and still and let the dog notice the other dog on their own. The instant they LOOK at it, click. When they turn back to you, treat. If they react, or don't turn back after the click, you are too close — move further away and reset. Goal: 3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance before moving to Level 2.
LEVEL 2 – DISENGAGE: Let them notice the dog, then wait 1–5 seconds to see if they look away on their own. The instant they DISENGAGE, click, then treat. If they fixate for more than 5 seconds, drop back to Level 1. Goal: 3–5 clean reps in a row, then move 1–5 steps closer. If the other dog is moving or changing intensity, go back to Level 1 at the new distance.

DOSAGE — this matters more than people think: play for 1–5 minutes, then take a break. Not 30 minutes. 2–3 short sessions per week is plenty, plus your quiet walks. Even sub-threshold exposure accumulates stress, so keep sessions brief and end on a win.

WHERE TO GET SAFE TRIGGERS: sit in your car with the boot open at a park entrance; stand well back from a school gate at pick-up time; the far corner of a field near a dog park. You want dogs at a predictable distance, not surprise ones.

BACK OFF the moment you see lip-licking, yawning out of context, scratching, whale eye, a frozen stare, or refusing food. Those are the early signals; the bark is the late one.

KEEP DOING: name game and U-turns daily; loose-leash walking on quiet streets, 10 min.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: dog reliably looks at a distant dog then back at you for a treat; you have shaved 10–20 ft off the week-1 working distance. Some weeks you will lose ground — that is normal, not failure.

subtasks.title: Week 3: class starts + closing the distance + the emergency plan
subtasks.description:
Goal: get the paid eyes on you, and build the routine you'll actually use when a dog appears round a corner.

CLASS: your reactive-dog class should start around now (South Bay Dog Training, Campbell, Sunday morning, $360 — details in the trainer subtask). Bring the working-distance number from week 1 and the notes from week 2 to the first session; it will save you 20 minutes of the trainer's time.

CONTINUE engage-disengage 2–3 sessions/week, moving 1–5 steps closer only after 3–5 clean reps. Never close distance twice in one session.

ADD — THE EMERGENCY U-TURN, rehearsed cold:
On quiet streets, practise the full sequence with no dog present: spot imaginary trigger → 'this way!' in a bright voice → pivot → jog 10 steps away → 'find it', scatter treats on the ground. Run it 5 times per walk until it's automatic for YOU. Your hands need to know it before you need it.

ADD — PATTERN GAMES for passing at closer range: '1-2-3' treat game (count out loud, treat on '3', repeat while walking past a trigger at distance). The rhythm gives the dog something predictable to do instead of scanning.

ADD — PARALLEL WALKING if you have a friend with a calm, neutral dog. Walk in the same direction, 50+ ft apart, gradually converging over several sessions. Never head-on, never nose-to-nose. This is far more valuable than another sidewalk pass.

LOOSE LEASH: move to 15–20 min walks with a mild distraction present. The rule stays absolute — tight leash means the walk stops.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: you can walk past a stationary dog at roughly half the week-1 distance with the dog eating and glancing at you; the U-turn happens without you having to think about it.

subtasks.title: Week 4: real-world walks, review the numbers, decide what's next
subtasks.description:
Goal: put it together on a normal walk, then honestly assess whether DIY-plus-class is enough.

DO:
- Two or three real neighbourhood walks at a moderately busy time, armed with the U-turn, 'find it', and the 1-2-3 game. Cross the street early, put parked cars between you and an approaching dog, use driveways as bays to let dogs pass. Managing the environment is a permanent skill, not a crutch you graduate from.
- Keep 2 engage-disengage sessions this week at your current closest successful distance. Don't chase a new record in week 4.
- Loose-leash: 20–30 min walks. By now the default should be a slack leash on quiet stretches.

REVIEW — compare week 4 against your written week 1 number:
- Working distance then vs now (feet).
- Outbursts per walk then vs now.
- Recovery time after an outburst then vs now. This is the most sensitive measure of progress — it usually improves before the barking does.

DECIDE:
- Distance closing, fewer outbursts, faster recovery → you're winning. Book the Level 2 / outdoor reactive class ($360 at South Bay Dog Training) and keep going. Realistic total timeline is 3–6 months, not 4 weeks.
- Flat or worse despite consistent work → book private 1:1 (In Tune Dog Training, or D For Dogz private coaching at $420 consult + $250/session). Also worth a vet visit: undiagnosed pain, thyroid issues, or poor sleep all lower the threshold for reactivity, and adolescent dogs are frequently under-slept. A border collie mix that isn't getting mental work will also be more reactive by default.

SET EXPECTATIONS: the goal is a dog who can walk past another dog calmly on leash. It is not necessarily a dog-park dog, and that is a perfectly good outcome. Some dogs simply prefer human company; pushing for dog-park friendliness usually backfires.
